facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Traditional Tibetan sources mention the existence of a great library at Nalanda named Dharmaganja (Piety Mart) which comprised three large multi-storeyed buildings, the Ratnasagara, the Ratnodadhi, and the Ratnaranjaka.
facts.source_name: Sumpa Mkhan-po, Pag Sam Jon Zang
facts.text: Tibetan historical chronicles describe Nalanda's central library quarter by the name Dharmaganja, stating it comprised three prominent multi-storeyed edifices named Ratnasagara, Ratnodadhi, and Ratnaranjaka.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Ratnodadhi was nine storeys high and housed the most sacred manuscripts including the Prajnyaparamita Sutra and the Guhyasamaja.
facts.source_name: Sumpa Mkhan-po, Pag Sam Jon Zang
facts.text: Tibetan records state that the Ratnodadhi library building stood nine storeys high and preserved the university's sacred scriptures, including the Prajnaparamita Sutra.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Given the three multi-story libraries, including a nine-storey one evidenced by literary records, 9 million is just a number. The actual number of books remains unknown.
facts.text: The widespread assertion that Nalanda's library contained nine million manuscripts is disputed by academic historians as an unverified modern estimation lacking contemporary inventory evidence.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Tabakat-i-Nasiri written by Minhaj-i-siraj does not mention the library being burnt down by Bakhtiyar Khilji, while the three months duration appears solely in later popular tradition.
facts.text: The popular claim that the Nalanda library burned for three months straight is disputed by historians, who note that primary thirteenth-century chronicles record the destruction of monasteries but make no mention of a three-month burning period.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: There were a great number of books there; and, when all these books came under the observation of the Musalmans, they summoned a number of Hindus that they might give them information respecting the import of those books; but the whole of the Hindus had been killed.
facts.text: Thirteenth-century Persian historian Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani recorded that Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji seized a fortified monastic compound in Bihar containing an immense collection of books whose readers had perished.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The text describes the capture of 'Bihar' (likely Odantapuri, adjacent to Nalanda), leading scholars to debate whether Nalanda itself or Odantapuri was the primary site targeted in that specific passage.
facts.text: Historians disagree on whether the college fortress sacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji in Minhaj-i-Siraj's chronicle was Nalanda or the adjacent fortified mahavihara of Odantapuri.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: When he visited Nalanda in 1235, he found it still surviving, but a ghost of its past existence... under the tutelage of Rahula Shribhadra.
facts.text: Tibetan monk Dharmasvamin visited Nalanda in 1235 CE, decades after Khalji's initial expedition, and documented that abbot Rahulasribhadra was still instructing seventy students amidst the damaged complex.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Excavations conducted by Archaeological Survey of India during 1915-37 and 1974-82 have exposed the extensive remains of six major brick temples and eleven monasteries arranged on a systematic layout.
facts.text: Excavations conducted by the Archaeological Survey of India between 1915 and 1937 exposed eleven monasteries and six major brick temples aligned along a central axis.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Archaeological evidence from ASI excavations corroborates this, revealing layers of ash and charred remains dated to the late 12th to early 13th century CE, indicating widespread burning.
facts.text: Archaeological excavations at Nalanda uncovered thick strata of ash, charred timber beams, and heat-altered bricks across monastery levels, providing physical proof of devastating fires.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The collection includes copper plates and stone inscriptions, coins, pottery and samples of burnt rice (12th century AD) found among the ruins here.
facts.text: Excavations at Nalanda recovered jars containing charred rice grains dating to the twelfth century CE, which are on display at the site museum.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: This site was the first to be excavated by ASI at Nalanda and revealed multi-layered construction periods exhibiting repetitive renovation over earlier strata.
facts.text: Stratigraphic investigations by the Archaeological Survey of India at Monastery Site Number 1 identified nine successive levels of construction and rebuilding across several centuries.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Xuanzang who studied there for five years, studied Yoga shastra under Silabhadra. He also studied Nyaya, Hetuvidya, Shabdavidya and the Sanskrit grammar of Panini.
facts.source_name: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions
facts.text: Chinese scholar-pilgrim Xuanzang spent five years residing and studying Buddhist logic and philosophy at Nalanda during the seventh century CE.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: For nine years they meditated and attained siddhi. On return they scattered charmed ashes all around and those ashes ignited the fire.
facts.source_name: Taranatha, History of Buddhism in India
facts.text: A seventeenth-century Tibetan legend recorded by Taranatha claims that two humiliated mendicants performed ascetic penance for nine years and threw magically energized embers that ignited the library complex.

scenes.vo: Ab aapse ek aasaan sawaal. Aapne Nalanda ke 3 mahine jalne ki baat kahan suni thi, school, ghar ya WhatsApp? Comment mein bataiye. Aur agar aap Nalanda gaye hain, toh bataiye wahan aapko sabse zyada kya yaad raha.
